evidence_add.extracted: For the BPRS hallucinatory-behaviour item, which is one of the three items of the positive subscale, the authors used the original, wider item description so that perceptual distortions as well as hallucinations could be scored on it, so this study's positive-subscale scores are not comparable with studies that score that item in the usual way and the rise cannot be read as evidence of hallucinations. In the Discussion the authors state that the study did not detect formal thought disorder or language disorganisation during the conditions tested, apart from modest effects on the alogia subscale of the negative-symptom scale, although blocking, loosening of associations and language disorganisation were noted during the loading period.

change: Review and adjudication, ketamine round: the opening frame no longer claims a salt-water comparison day for the open study that had none, and the duration sentence is limited to the studies that rated symptoms after the infusion stopped (second reader 226 on Vollenweider et al., 1997b). Malhotra's item spread is no longer labelled SD, because the paper does not label it, and its unchanged hostility-suspiciousness score and its last rating time are now stated (second reader 225). Krystal's illusions sentence now carries the ideas of reference and loosening of associations reported on the same page. Newcomer's 'measured steady blood levels' is now 'fixed infusions aimed at steady blood levels', and a new anchor records that its hallucinatory-behaviour item was widened to count perceptual distortions and that it detected no formal thought disorder. The Beck et al. (2020) figures and the certainty rating were not adjudicated in this round: that web source has not yet had its second reading.

evidence_set: Free recall of a 12-word categorical list was lower on the ketamine day than on the salt-water day in 15 healthy volunteers: drug F1,14 = 9.63 (p = .008), time F4,56 = 5.16 (p = .005), drug x time F4,52 = 4.35 (p = .004); lower at 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.79 (p = .001) and at 90 minutes F1,13 = 6.25 (p = .026). Recognition of the same words (n = 14) was lower too: drug F1,13 = 17.48 (p = .001), time F4,52 = 6.05, drug x time F4,52 = 7.95 (p < .001), lower at 10 minutes F1,13 = 8.92 (p = .01) and 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.78. The attention score fell less markedly: drug x time F4,56 = 2.71 (p = .05), lower at 55 minutes only, F1,14 = 8.79 (p = .01). The paper's individual counts at 55 minutes of the ketamine infusion are falls from each person's own pre-infusion level on that day, not differences from the salt-water day: 13 of 15 for free recall, 9 of 14 for recognition and 9 of 15 for attention. All three measures come from the same word list, so they are not independent of each other.
change: Review and adjudication, ketamine round: the three individual counts are stated as falls from each person's own pre-infusion level on the ketamine day, in the statement, the magnitude and anchor 0, because that is what the source says (second reader 225, blind reading and targeted check, confirmed on the rendered p. 303). 'Recover within about an hour or two' becomes 'no longer detectably lower about an hour after the end', limited to the one study that tested after the infusion stopped, since neither of the other two did (second reader 225 on Newcomer et al., 1999). Newcomer's 'measured steady blood levels' is now 'fixed infusions aimed at steady blood levels', with what was actually measured. The Krystal sentence names the 14 to 16 people behind each cognitive result, and the correlation range now covers all six printed values.

evidence_set: Twenty minutes after the injection, on haloperidol, the BPRS total was 33.4 (6.0) after salt water and 38.3 (7.1), 39.3 (5.0) and 45.3 (7.7) after 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg, significant at 0.3 (p = .005) and 0.5 mg/kg (p = .01), against baselines of 34.6 (7.0), 33.2 (4.2), 35.2 (5.4) and 36.9 (11.0); n = 9, 9, 9 and 7. The three psychosis items carried the change: 8.0 (3.1) after salt water against 9.8 (3.3) (p = .05), 9.3 (2.8) and 12.3 (2.5) (p = .02), from baselines of 8.1, 6.8, 6.6 and 6.9. At 90 and 180 minutes the total is at or below its own baseline in every condition (at 0.5 mg/kg, 32.3 and 32.3), while the psychosis score at 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg is 7.0 at both times, just above baselines of 6.8 and 6.6, and Table 2 marks the 0.1 mg/kg value at 180 minutes significant although it sits below the salt-water value of 7.9. The paper nowhere says whether the figures in brackets are standard deviations or standard errors; they make sense only as standard deviations. No test statistic, degrees of freedom, interval or effect size is printed.

evidence_add.locator: Abstract, last third (p. 9); Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, last paragraph (p. 12); Table 3, column heading 'Delayed Drug Effects' and its entries (p. 14)
evidence_add.extracted: The paper gives the timing of the later reports in three incompatible ways: the abstract calls them delayed or prolonged effects at 8 to 24 hours, the results say the delusions came back about 6 to 8 hours after the injection, and the heading of the table that lists them per person reads 4 to 24 hours, while that table's own entries record one episode lasting 12 hours, dreaming over two nights and visual phenomena recurring over several days. Nothing in the paper reconciles the three windows.

change: Review and adjudication, ketamine round: the claim no longer says that every score was back at or below its own baseline at 90 and 180 minutes. That holds for the BPRS total in all four conditions but not for the psychosis subscale at 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg, where 7.0 at both times sits just above baselines of 6.8 and 6.6 (second reader 225, partly-supported; checked on Table 2 rendered at 150 dpi). The statement now says that two of the nine never received the largest amount and were given a blinded salt-water injection in its place, which is why seven people contributed to it; that the paper does not label the figures in brackets as standard deviations or standard errors; and, with a new anchor, where its three different windows for the later reports are printed.
